title: Explorers and Expeditions
objectives: I can explain ten words about travel, exploring, and finding the way.
I can use context to tell how a trip, a path, or a place is described.
I can use the endings -tion and -er/-or to understand words about people and actions.
I can write a short account of a journey using exact words.
rationale: Exploration language appears in history, geography, and adventure fiction. The ten words sort into kinds of trips (expedition, voyage, caravan, trek), finding the way (compass, navigate, destination), and land and daring (wilderness, terrain, venture). The unit also gives students a setting for sequence signal words from unit 2, and it revisits adventurous from unit 1. The passage is a short invented story, so every detail about the trip is safe to teach as fiction while the vocabulary stays accurate.

words.def: A long trip taken for a special purpose, such as exploring.
words.ex: The scientists' expedition to the Arctic lasted three months.
words.ex2: Our class planned an expedition to the pond to count frogs.
words.nonExample: A quick walk to the mailbox is not an expedition.

apps.academic: In history, an expedition set out to map land that no one had charted.
apps.spoken: We're going on an expedition to look for fossils.
apps.writing: Use expedition for a planned trip with a goal, such as discovery.

cloze.s: The ___ to find the lost city took the team through jungles and across rivers for many months.

cloze2.s: Before the ___ to the pond, we packed nets, notebooks, and rain jackets.

misuse.s: Our expedition was a two-minute walk from the kitchen to the refrigerator.
misuse.why: An expedition is a long, planned trip with a purpose; a walk to the refrigerator is neither.

visual.alt: A compass next to a pair of hiking boots.

words.frame: An expedition could go to ___ to ___.

words.def: A long trip, especially one by sea or through space.
words.ex: The voyage across the ocean took the ship six weeks.
words.ex2: The astronauts began their voyage to the moon at dawn.
words.nonExample: A ten-minute bus ride to school is not a voyage.

apps.academic: A social studies text may describe the voyage of early settlers across an ocean.
apps.spoken: I get seasick just thinking about a long voyage.
apps.writing: Use voyage for a long trip over water or through space.

cloze.s: The ship's ___ across the stormy sea lasted forty days before it reached land.

cloze2.s: On the long ___ to the island, the passengers watched whales from the deck.

misuse.s: My voyage to the corner store took one minute, and I never left the sidewalk.
misuse.why: A voyage is a long trip, usually by sea or through space; a one-minute walk is not.

visual.alt: A sailboat riding a wave on the open sea.

words.def: A tool with a needle that always points north.
words.ex: The scout checked her compass before leaving the trail.
words.ex2: Mari held the compass level so the needle could swing freely.
words.nonExample: A clock tells the hour, not the direction, so it is not a compass.

apps.academic: A map and a compass help hikers tell which way is north, south, east, and west.
apps.spoken: My compass says we're walking east.
apps.writing: Use compass for the tool, and name the direction it shows.

cloze.s: Because the ___ needle always points north, the hikers knew which way to walk.

cloze2.s: Without a map or a ___, the sailors could not tell which way was east.

misuse.s: The hiker looked at her compass to see what time it was.
misuse.why: A compass shows direction, not time.

visual.alt: A round compass and a map.

words.def: To find the way and steer along a path.
words.ex: Mina used the map to navigate through the crowded train station.
words.ex2: Sailors long ago learned to navigate by watching the stars.
words.nonExample: Wandering with no plan and no map is not navigating.

apps.academic: To navigate a river, a boat captain must know where the shallow places are.
apps.spoken: I can navigate with the map on my phone.
apps.writing: Use navigate for finding and following a route.

cloze.s: With only a map and a flashlight, the campers had to ___ through the dark forest.

cloze2.s: Before computers, sailors learned to ___ by watching the sun and the stars.

misuse.s: The pilot navigated across the ocean by closing her eyes and spinning the wheel.
misuse.why: To navigate is to find the way carefully; spinning the wheel with eyes shut does not.

visual.alt: A map and a ship heading across the water.

words.def: The place a person or thing is going to.
words.ex: The family's destination was a cabin by the lake.
words.ex2: The package reached its destination two days early.
words.nonExample: The place where you start is not your destination.

apps.academic: On a map, mark the starting point and the destination before planning the route.
apps.spoken: Our destination is only ten minutes away.
apps.writing: Use destination for the place a trip is heading toward.

cloze.s: After a long day on the train, we finally reached our ___ in the city by the sea.

cloze2.s: Once the bus arrives at its ___, every passenger must get off.

misuse.s: Our destination was the town where we started, so we never left home.
misuse.why: A destination is the place you are going; the starting place is not it.

visual.alt: A checkered flag next to a map pin.

words.def: A natural area with no towns, where few or no people live.
words.ex: The hikers walked for days in the wilderness without seeing a road.
words.ex2: Bears and wolves live in the wilderness of the northern forest.
words.nonExample: A busy city park with paved paths is not wilderness.

apps.academic: A national park protects wilderness so that plants and animals can live undisturbed.
apps.spoken: We camped deep in the wilderness.
apps.writing: Use wilderness for a wild place with no towns or roads.

cloze.s: No roads, houses, or stores were nearby; the campers were deep in the ___ for a week.

cloze2.s: Few people had ever walked through the ___ north of the river, and the trails were faint.

misuse.s: She lived in the wilderness, a crowded city with a hundred stores on every block.
misuse.why: A wilderness has very few people; a crowded city is the opposite.

visual.alt: Tall pine trees in front of a mountain.

words.frame: In the wilderness you might see ___.

words.def: A group of travelers or animals moving together on a long trip.
words.ex: A caravan of camels crossed the desert at dawn.
words.ex2: The pioneers traveled in a caravan of wagons so they could help each other.
words.nonExample: One person walking alone is not a caravan.

apps.academic: In history, trade caravans carried goods across long distances on land.
apps.spoken: A caravan of cars followed the bus.
apps.writing: Use caravan for travelers moving together in a line or group.

cloze.s: A ___ of loaded camels crossed the dry desert, tied together from one animal to the next.

cloze2.s: The pioneers traveled in a ___ of wagons so that they could help each other on the trail.

misuse.s: The lone traveler rode by himself, forming a caravan with no one else.
misuse.why: A caravan is a group traveling together; one person alone is not a caravan.

visual.alt: A line of camels crossing a sandy desert.

words.def: To go or do something that may be risky.
words.ex: The kittens ventured out of the box for the first time.
words.ex2: Few sailors dared to venture beyond the harbor in that storm.
words.nonExample: Staying safely inside is not venturing.

apps.academic: Early explorers ventured into unmapped land with little more than a compass.
apps.spoken: I'll venture outside when the rain stops.
apps.writing: Use venture for a brave step toward something unknown.

cloze.s: The brave hikers decided to ___ into the cave even though the entrance was dark and narrow.

cloze2.s: The shy kitten finally began to ___ out from under the bed into the bright room.

misuse.s: She ventured to the far side of the river by never leaving her chair.
misuse.why: To venture is to go toward something risky; staying in a chair is not.

visual.alt: A kitten stepping out of a cardboard box.

words.def: The shape and surface of the land in a place.
words.ex: The hikers slowed down on the rocky terrain.
words.ex2: Tractors with big tires can drive across muddy terrain.
words.nonExample: The weather on a trail is not the terrain; terrain is the land itself.

apps.academic: Geographers describe terrain as flat, hilly, mountainous, or rocky.
apps.spoken: The terrain was bumpy, so we slowed down.
apps.writing: Use terrain to describe what the land is like under your feet.

cloze.s: The jeep bounced over the rocky ___, where big stones covered the hills.

cloze2.s: Mountain bikers prefer rough ___ with steep hills and sharp turns.

misuse.s: The terrain was a warm breeze that blew in from the west.
misuse.why: Terrain is the land, not the wind or the weather.

visual.alt: A mountain with large rocks at its base.

words.def: To make a long, hard trip on foot.
words.ex: The hikers trekked up the mountain, resting only twice.
words.ex2: We had to trek three miles through deep snow to reach the cabin.
words.nonExample: Riding a bus to school is not trekking.

apps.academic: Explorers had to trek for weeks across land that had no roads.
apps.spoken: We'll trek to the waterfall tomorrow morning.
apps.writing: Use trek for long walking trips that take effort.

cloze.s: The explorers had to ___ for days through deep snow because no roads reached the village.

cloze2.s: Every summer, the scouts ___ twelve miles to the lake carrying heavy packs.

misuse.s: We trekked to the next room in two steps and sat down.
misuse.why: To trek is to make a long, hard trip; two steps is neither long nor hard.

passage.title: The Map With a Blank Space
paras: Mapmaker Elena Cruz joined an expedition to chart a mountain valley that appeared on no map. The team's destination was a lake that local guides called Silver Water. To reach it, the group first made a voyage across a wide river in two flat boats.

On the far shore, a caravan of twelve mules waited to carry food, tents, and tools. The group would trek for ten days through wilderness without a single road. Each night, Elena checked her compass, because clouds often hid the sun and the stars.

The terrain grew harder every day. Loose stones slid under the mules' hooves, and the trail climbed steeply between cliffs. On the sixth day, thick fog covered the path. "We must navigate by the compass alone," said the guide, Mr. Reyes. The team moved slowly, and eventually the fog lifted.

Some members wanted to turn back, but Elena decided to venture ahead and scout a safer path. She climbed a ridge and saw a bright strip of water in the distance. It was Silver Water. When she shouted the news, the whole team cheered.
On the tenth day they set up camp on the shore. Elena drew the lake and the trail on a clean sheet, and the blank space on the map was gone.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "trek" most nearly means
choices: make a long, hard journey on foot
qs.why: The team walks for ten days through wilderness with no road, so trek means a long hard trip on foot.

qs.q: Why does Elena check her compass each night?
choices: Clouds often hide the sun and the stars, so she needs another way to know direction.
It shows her where the mules are.
qs.why: The text says clouds often hid the sun and the stars, so the compass was her guide.

qs.q: Why does Mr. Reyes say the team must navigate by the compass alone?
choices: Fog hides the path and landmarks, so the compass is their only guide.
He wants to teach Elena how to read a map.
The mules cannot walk without a compass.
qs.why: Fog covers the path, so they cannot see where they are going without the compass.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that the terrain was hard to cross?
choices: The group crossed a wide river in flat boats.
Elena drew the lake on a clean sheet.
Local guides called the lake Silver Water.
Loose stones slid under the mules' hooves, and the trail climbed steeply between cliffs.
qs.why: Sliding stones and steep trails show that the land was difficult.

qs.q: Which sentence tells the main idea of the passage?
choices: An expedition team used careful travel and courage to find and map a hidden lake.
Fog is dangerous in the mountains.
qs.why: The story shows the team crossing hard land, finding the lake, and filling in the map.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten exploration words, read a story about a team crossing rough land, notice the endings -tion and -er, and write about journeys using exact travel words.

notes.va.expedition.n: An expedition has a purpose, such as science or discovery. Contrast it with a trip to the store.
notes.va.voyage.n: Voyage suggests a long trip, by sea or through space. Use maps of ocean routes to show scale.
notes.va.compass.n: Bring a real compass if you can and have students find north. Remind them it shows direction, not location.
notes.va.navigate.v: Students often think navigate needs a screen. Show that map, compass, stars, and landmarks can all help.
notes.va.destination.n: The destination is where you are going. Practice by giving a start and a destination and asking students for the route.
notes.va.wilderness.n: Wilderness is a wild area. Ask students whether a city park counts; it does not, since wilderness has few people and no roads.
notes.va.caravan.n: Use a picture of camels roped in a line. Ask: why travel together instead of alone?
notes.va.venture.v: Venture is a verb for a risky step. Mention that venture as a noun means a business project, which is a later meaning.
notes.va.terrain.n: Terrain is the surface of the land. Have students sort terrain words such as rocky, hilly, muddy, and flat.
notes.va.trek.v: Trek means long and hard. Students may use trek for any walk; ask how long and how hard it must be.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The team can't see the trail in the fog. Mr. Reyes says to navigate by the compass alone. Navigate means to find the way, so the compass is their only guide. I can use navigate in my own sentence: With the compass, we could navigate through the fog.'

misconceptions: A voyage is only a trip by ship.
Navigate means to drive a car.

teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit expedition, voyage, and trek as three kinds of trips two days later, again at one week, and reuse adventurous and eventually when students describe travelers.

wida.oral: Partner A names a trip without saying the word. Partner B guesses whether it is an expedition, voyage, trek, or caravan and says why.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (zona salvaje for wilderness, hacer una larga caminata for trek, aventurarse, brújula) not reviewed by a native speaker; wilderness has no single common Spanish word.
The passage is invented fiction; no historical claims are made.
Venture is taught only as a verb; the noun sense (a business project) is left for a later grade.
